extracted.intended_audience: first-time listeners / newcomers to the Welcome to Night Vale podcast
extracted.subtask_description: A starter's guide for new listeners to the fiction podcast Welcome to Night Vale, recommending how to begin, which episodes/series are safe entry points, and what kinds of episodes exist. Advises on standalone material, companion recap show, and highlights exemplar episodes and short series.

rubrics_metrics.name: You can start with any episode / skip around
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t be! You can start listening to Welcome to Night Vale with any episode, and you should feel free to skip around, or move backwards. Time is weird, so your listening experience can be, too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide explicitly tells newcomers that episodes are approachable out of order; there is no required linear listening. Use your curiosity — pick any episode that appeals and jump in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novels and live shows are standalone
rubrics_metrics.description: Plus, the novels and live shows are completely standalone stories, so you can go read, watch, or listen to any of them without having to know anything about the show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you prefer novels or live recordings to podcast episodes, consume them independently; they won't spoil or require prior episode knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Good Morning Night Vale recap show as a first-time-listener companion
rubrics_metrics.description: We also have a recap show called Good Morning Night Vale. Each episode is a deep dive into one episode of Welcome to Night Vale, starting with the very first episode from 2012. It's a great audio companion for a first time listener, and you can subscribe right here.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want episode-by-episode context or a guided listening path through the series, follow the recap podcast which analyzes individual episodes in order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer curated single episodes and short series as safe entry points
rubrics_metrics.description: We've collected some of our favorite episodes below. These single episodes and short series are stand-alone. You won't be spoiled if you decide you love them so much you want to start from the beginning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page lists specific single episodes (e.g., 13, 26, 33, 42, 60, 67, 71, 79, 174, 188, 190, 216, 224, 239, 272) and short series as recommended, because they function independently and are good introductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episode tone and theme vary—pick by the kind of story you want
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes range from intimate/second-person ('A Story About You'), creepy (e.g., 'Faceless Old Woman', 'Cassette'), character-focused pieces, whimsical or conspiratorial episodes, to episodes about independence, community, or horoscopes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose episodes matching desired tone: for creepy stories try 26 or 33; for introspective/character backstory try 33 or 216; for thematic episodes about independence and conspiracies try 42; for horoscopes/segment-driven episodes try 272. The guide annotates each recommended episode with its tone/theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect formal/structural experimentation in some episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: Some episodes play with the podcast format (e.g., 60 'Water Failure' uses an automated phone tree; 67 '[Best Of?]' is a fake 'best of' composed of impossible clips; 272 is the horoscopes segment expanded).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you enjoy format experiments or meta-podcast humor, seek out episodes the guide flags as format-play. Notes include production trivia (e.g., the phone tree voice was done in a single uninterrupted take).

rubrics_metrics.name: Short series often tell a single event from different perspectives or form self-contained arcs
rubrics_metrics.description: Short series listed (e.g., The Sandstorm — same event told from two cities' points of view; eGemony — a three-parter by a guest novelist; A matter of blood; The Birthday of Lee Marvin; The Blood/Space War) are self-contained and stand entirely on their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you like multi-episode story arcs, the guide recommends these short series as entry points; they usually focus on a specific event or character arc and do not require broader series knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guest writers and guest voices are notable and often produce standalone favorites
rubrics_metrics.description: Several recommended episodes/series are written by or feature guest writers/voices (e.g., 'Faceless Old Woman' features Mara Wilson; 'Cassette' and other stories by guest writers like Zack Parsons; eGemony by Glen David Gold; Radio Jupiter features Robin Virginie).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episodes credited to guest creators often have distinctive voices or formats; the guide highlights these as fan favorites and safe entry points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-focused episodes and arcs are accessible introductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes that center on specific characters (e.g., 'The Ball is where the win is' about Steve Carlsberg; 'Abby Palmer tells all' about Cecil's sister; The Birthday of Lee Marvin) provide intimate looks at Night Vale inhabitants and make approachable ways to enter the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you prefer character-driven stories, pick episodes or short series that spotlight beloved or intriguing characters; these are highlighted as exemplars of the show's human (or town) scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta / creator-interaction episodes exist and may be idiosyncratic entry points
rubrics_metrics.description: Some episodes depart from fiction to feature creators or community-focused content (e.g., 188 'Listener Questions' where co-creator Joseph Fink answers questions; 190 a celebration of podcasting with many guest voices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These meta episodes can be unusual and may not follow typical narrative structure; they can still be enjoyable as standalone curiosities but may be less representative of the usual fiction episodes.
